description: When a picture, diagram or animation is explained by narration, adding on-screen text that repeats the narration word for word is expected to lower transfer for novices, most in system-paced lessons; when no picture competes for the eyes, the same words spoken and written do no harm and help second-language, less fluent and low-prior-knowledge readers, and text that helps novices becomes redundant as expertise grows. Claims test this: Mayer's experiments, a meta-analysis of verbal redundancy, a 63-study review and a meta-meta-analysis, with boundary conditions for pictures, pacing, reader fluency, prior knowledge, outcome and age.
title: Redundancy Principle

description: For a learner who has just performed a task or acted in a practice setting, structured prompts to examine that performance against a stated criterion and commit to a change are expected to improve later performance more than unguided reflection, qualified by the learner's ability to judge their own work, access to feedback, and whether the planned change is acted on.
title: Reflection

description: For learners whose ideas on a concept or principle may diverge from the plan, a teacher who makes their thinking visible, reads it against a prepared model of likely ideas and chooses the next move from it is expected to improve conceptual understanding and near transfer over the same plan delivered unchanged; no claim in the wiki tests this directly.
title: Responsive Teaching

description: For learners who have studied material, recalling it from memory rather than restudying tends to raise delayed retention when initial retrieval mostly succeeds or is corrected by feedback; restudy can lead at a few minutes, transfer gains are smaller and conditional, and high element-interactivity material is contested.
title: Retrieval Practice
